courses.subject: LING
courses.title: Exploring Grammar: Cantonese
courses.description: This course introduces the basic features of Cantonese grammar taking a primarily descriptive approach. The areas covered include Cantonese phonology, morphology, aspectual system, grammatical constructions and sentence final particles. Students should develop a sharpened sensitivity to the characteristics of Cantonese grammar and be able to appreciate its complexities and their own intuitions about the language.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken CHLL3162
courses.learning_outcomes:
- Have a better understanding of the value of the studies of Cantonese and its grammar in linguistics and multilingual societies
- Become familiar with common grammatical concepts and terms, with reference to the traditional grammatical framework and the generative framework
- Describe language phenomena and apply the grammatical concepts to analyzing the phonological, morphological and syntactic structures of Cantonese
- Become familiar with the salient grammatical features of Cantonese and the similarity and differences between Cantonese and Mandarin
courses.course_syllabus:
Topic

Contents/ Fundamental concepts

Linguistic status of Cantonese
Dialects vs. Languages, Cantonese as a Chinese dialect(?!), multi-lingual society, value of Cantonese in linguistics research

Phonology
Descriptive vs. prescriptive (正音), Cantonese phonological system, tones, phonotactic rules, dialectal variations, Jyutping

Morphology
Classification of morphological structure in traditional Chinese grammar, e.g. 偏正, 動補, 並列, etc., word categories, tagging

Topic comment structure
Contrast between subject- vs. topic-prominent languages (e.g. English and Cantonese), various constraints of topicalization

Sentence particles
Sentence particles vs phrase particles, semantics and pragmatics of particles

Nominals and Classifiers
Nominal structure, classifier types, (in)definiteness of nominals, differences between Cantonese and Mandarin

Verbal suffixes/ particles
Syntax and semantics of zo 咗, gwo 過, gan 緊, hoi 開, faan 翻, etc.

Ditransitive construction
Word order of ditransitive, Thematic roles, weight

Wh-interpretation
Various use of wh-words in Cantonese, e.g. wh-indefinite, negative wh-words, wh-placeholders, surprise wh¬-interpretation, etc.

Right Dislocation
Focus, syntax of sentence particles and implications to Chinese clausal structure

courses.subject: LING
courses.title: Phonetics II
courses.description: This course builds on the phonetic knowledge acquired through LING2003. Issues in speech production and speech perception research will be introduced. Emphasis will be placed on acoustic analysis of speech sounds. Students will gain a solid knowledge of the physical nature of speech sounds and be familiar with the various connected speech processes. Students will gain hands-on experience of phonetic research in the form of a mini-project.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Prerequisite: LING2003.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students will have a good understanding of the complex nature of speech communication.

2. Students will be familiar with the major issues in both speech production and speech perception.

3. Students will be familiar with the acoustic properties of different types of consonants and vowels.

4. Students will acquire the skills for acoustic analysis, and learn how to use Praat for such analysis.

5. Students will develop independent research skills and critical thinking skills by doing a small group project on a topic of their choice.

6. Students will be ready to conduct further phonetic study, e.g. for their senior research thesis.

courses.subject: LING
courses.title: Phonology II
courses.description: This course focuses on the development of phonological theory, looking at general issues in the areas of tone, stress, syllable, prosody, and their interactions within the framework of autosegmental phonology. Students will learn how to analyse data from different languages, draw generalizations from a crosslinguistic perspective, and account for phonological patterns adequately.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Prerequisite: LING2004
courses.learning_outcomes:
• Understand basic concepts of prosody, such as tone, duration, syllable, and stress

• Understand how segments are organized into prosodic unit

• Understand how prosody interact with segmental phonology

• Be able to identify key factors that trigger prosodic processes

• Be able to apply phonological concepts into data analysis

courses.subject: LING
courses.title: Syntax II
courses.description: Taking universal grammar to be a biologically based system within the language faculty of the human mind, the course aims to illustrate how constituent structures in syntax are generated and combined to form legitimate syntactic derivations, how lexical properties and pragmatics motivate syntax, and how relevant syntactic theories can attain explanatory power in addressing the hierarchical, generative, recursive and virtually infinite nature of the language system. Students will be trained to apply syntactic theories in their analysis of data drawn from various languages, formulate structural arguments, and confirm their arguments based on further empirical investigation.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Prerequisite: LING2005
courses.course_syllabus:
1) The Generative Enterprise: P&P modal (revision)
- Innateness of Language Faculty
- Linguistics as a cognitive science
- Mental grammar
- Principles and Parameters modal
2) X'-Theory (revision)
- Phrase structure
- X’-theory (Why? How?)
- Projections: NP, DP, VP, vP, IP/TP, CP, etc.
3) Theta Theory
- Thematic structure
- Theta role assignment, -criterion
- Argument structures
- A-positions, -positions

4) Case Theory
- Theory of abstract Case
- Government
- Case filter, Visibility Hypothesis
- NP-movement, VP-subject-internal hypothesis
- Burzio’s generalization
- ECM verbs
- Dative shift
- DP hypothesis

5) Binding Theory (revision)
- Binding conditions
- Coreference, referential dependency
- Anaphora, pronouns, referential expressions
- Control vs. Raising

6) Movement Theory
- A-movement/NP-movement
- Head-movement, Head-Movement Constraint
- A'-movement, A'-positions, A'-dependency
- Wh-movement, relativization, topicalization
- Crossover effects (strong, weak)
- Reconstruction effects
7) Locality
- Subjacency, barriers
- Island constraints, island types (strong, weak)
- Empty Category Principle (ECP), intermediate traces
- Condition on Extraction Domain (CED)
- Parasitic gap, adjunct island
- Across-The-Board movement, coordination island
8) Logical Form
- Quantifiers: , 
- Quantifier Raising (QR)
- LF-movement
- Indefinites

courses.subject: LING
courses.title: Comparative Grammar
courses.description: This course aims at introducing to students a number of major similarities and differences between Chinese and other languages of interest. The emphasis will be on the basic grammatical characteristics of these languages. The lectures and discussions are intended to increase students’ sensitivity toward linguistic forms through practice in comparative and contrastive analyses. Students are encouraged to investigate languages of their interest and explore the typological differences between these languages through independent or collaborative work with their peers.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Prerequisite: LING2005
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Enhance students’ sensitivity toward linguistic universals and variations.

2. Heighten students’ awareness of the linguistic universals and variations manifested in English, Mandarin and other languages of interest, and deepen their appreciation of a comparative approach to language study.

3. Gain basic analytic and research skills in comparative studies.
courses.course_syllabus:
LING3107

| | Topic | Contents/ Fundamental concepts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Introduction | - Comparative approaches to language study -The principles & parameters in syntactic theory -Universal Grammar |
| Nominal structure I: The DP hypothesis | - NP vs. DP - The DP hypothesis - The syntactic statuses of articles & demostratives |
| Nominal structure II: Nominal expressions in Mandarin & Cantonese | - Two competing analyses of nominal expressions in Mandarin & Cantonese: i) the DP hypothesis, and ii) the CIP hypothesis |
| Nominal structure III: Adjectives | - Three analyses of adjectives: i) adjectives as heads selecting NPs; ii) adjunction analysis; iii) adjectives as Specifiers of FPs |
| Nominal structure IV: Adjectival modification in Mandarin | - Attributive adjectival modification in Mandarin: Compunds or Phrases? |
| Wh-movement | - Wh-question formation in English - Wh-movement |
| Wh in-situ | - LF movement - Non-movement and unselective binding - Wh-indefinites |
| Passives | - Passivization in English - Long and short passives in Mandarin |
| Clausal structure I: The Spilt-CP hypothesis | - The structure of CP - Topic and focus - Operator vs. non-operator |
| Clausal structure II: Topic structures in Mandarin | - Definitions of topics - Classification of topic structures - Movement or base-generation |
| Clausal structure III: Focus structures in Mandarin | - Definition of focus - Syntactic properties of focus in Mandarin |

courses.subject: LING
courses.title: First Language Acquisition
courses.description: This course introduces issues in the study of first language acquisition from a linguistic perspective. The topics covered include universal stages in first language acquisition, examining the child’s phonological, lexical and syntactic development and language socialization. Major theories of language acquisition and the critical period hypothesis will be examined and evaluated. While the primary focus of the course is on monolingual acquisition, issues in the study of children acquiring two first languages simultaneously will also be addressed.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students will gain an appreciation of innate and biological influences on language acquisition, and develop an understanding of the developmental milestones in first language acquisition. The course provides students with opportunities to conduct first-hand child language observation and data collection, and familiarizes students with some basic methods for analyzing child language data.
courses.course_syllabus:
LING3201

| | Topic | Contents/ Fundamental concepts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Biological foundations of language | Innateness; learning by instinct; language faculty; critical period; maturation; selective language impairment. |
| The nature of language acquisition | Input; caretaker speech; positive and negative evidence; adult linguistic competence. |
| The nativist approach to language learning | Learnability; the argument from poverty of stimulus; Universal grammar; abstract linguistic rules and structures. |
| Empiricist approaches to language learning | Cognitive principles for language learning; limited scope formulas; usage-based models of language learning; verb islands and lexically based patterns; connectionist approaches to language acquisition. |
| Methods in the study of language acquisition | Naturalistic and experimental methods; methods for eliciting language production; methods for testing language comprehension. |
| Early lexical/semantic development | Word spurt; indeterminacy in children's word meanings; innate biases for learning the meanings of words; early noun bias in lexical development. |
| Morphological acquisition | The acquisition of (regular or irregular) morphological rules; overgeneralizations; constraints on word formation. |
| The acquisition of categories and clause structure | Criteria for determining the acquisition of syntactic categories; abstract categories vs. lexically-based patterns. |
| Further on the acquisition of categories and clause structure | The onset of functional categories in various languages; the continuity hypothesis in grammatical development; the development of inflection. |
| Pro-drop in child grammar | Parameter setting in language development; Pro-drop in child and adult languages. |
| Children's knowledge of syntactic constraints | Universal constraints on phrase structure, binding and anaphora. |
| Phonological acquisition | Jakobson's discontinuity theory of phonological development; phonological rules in children's speech; target language influence on infant speech perception and production. |
| Pragmatic development: The acquisition of definite/indefinite reference | Linguistic form, word order and the signaling of (in)definiteness; referential knowledge of speaker and hearer; thematic structure in narrative patterns. |

courses.subject: LING
courses.title: Psycholinguistics
courses.description: This course studies language as a cognitive system which interfaces with other subsystems of mind. It examines the biological foundations of language and the nature of language competence from an evolutionary and developmental perspective. The ways in which language, thought and culture interact are explored. Emphasis will be placed on the principles and mechanisms that underlie speech perception, sentence processing and discourse comprehension, as well as structural factors in language production.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken PSYC3430
courses.course_syllabus:
Topic

Contents/ Fundamental concepts

unique features of natural languages
human languages versus animal communications

biological foundations of language
vocal tract structure, brain lateralization, aphasia, ‘language gene’

psychological mechanisms
memory, different types of processing

speech perception
categorical perception, the McGurk effect, models of speech perception

perception of written language
different writing systems, eye movements during reading, inner speech, models of word recognition

the mental lexicon
dimensions of word knowledge, organisation of the lexicon

utterance comprehension
garden path sentences, structural ambiguity

discourse comprehension

reference, coreference, genre, schema and discourse processing

language production
speech errors, linguistic plans

language and culture
language and thought, colour terms, taboos

courses.subject: LING
courses.title: Language and Mind
courses.description: This course explores central issues of language and cognition by investigating the complex relationships between language, thought and culture from an evolutionary and developmental perspective. How did language evolve as a component of mind in the history of mankind? How does language develop in the individual in relation to other cognitive capacities? In what ways is the organization of language similar to and distinct from other systems of cognition? To what extent does habitual thought depend on language, and to what extent does language enhance thought? These issues will be addressed, with emphasis on the interfaces between language structure and conceptual systems in the expression of reference, time, space, quantification, and modality.
courses.learning_outcomes:
- Students will have a good understanding of the relationship between language and the mind
- Students will learn how languages help to shape cognition/perception and how language involves as a result of our cognitive/perceptual habits
- Students will be critically aware of individual/cultural differences in language use
- Students will develop empirical skills to evaluate how language and other cognitive systems may interact
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Relation between language and mind
An overview of how language and mind/cognition can interact with each other

2. Language and other communication systems (iconicity)
How language and other communicative systems relate and differ; how iconicity shapes and develops in language and in the mid

3. Language in the deaf/blind
How is language represented and processed in the deaf and the blind

4. Language and memory
How does language and memory interact in the mind

5. Language and theory of mind
What role does language play in the theory of mind, in the understanding of other people’s state of mind?

6. Language and body
Whether and how linguistic information make use of the bodily states

7. Language and perception/cognition
Whether and how language interacts with the perception/cognition of space, colour, smell, time etc; the Whorf hypothesis

8. Bilingual mind
Whether and how learning to speak a second language may change cognition/mind

9. Language and culture
How different cultures use language differently

courses.subject: LING
courses.title: Second Language Acquisition
courses.description: The course introduces students to the field of second language acquisition (SLA) and the research issues related to the development of learners’ language systems. Topics include theories of second language acquisition and cross-linguistic influence. Comparisons will be made between first and second language acquisition. Students will gain a solid understanding of the issues and methods adopted in current research.
courses.learning_outcomes:
• develop understanding of different theoretical perspectives proposed to describe and explain the process of second language acquisition and learning

• understand the role that individual and social variables play in language acquisition and learning

• think critically the effective ways to acquire a second language

• explore the implications of SLA theories and research findings for language teaching

• develop ability to conduct research on a SLA topic of the student’s choice
courses.course_syllabus:
LING3204

| | Topic | Contents/ Fundamental concepts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Historical overview of SLA research | Introduction to the key concepts and issues and the overview of the recent history of SLA research |
| Comparisons between L1 and L2 acquisition | The differences between first and second language acquisition, and the role of the first language and age to second language acquisition |
| Learner language | Introduction to interlanguage and basic methods of error analysis |
| Language universals | Introduction and evaluation of universal grammar-based approaches to SLA |
| Cognitive theories | Introduction and evaluation of theories of L2 processing, connectionism, including their views of language, language learning, and the language learners. |
| Input and interaction | The role of environmental language in promoting L2 learning, including the input received by the learner, L2 output produced by the learner, and L2 interaction between the learner and the conversational partner. |
| Socio-cultural influences | Introduction to L2 learning as a situated social practice. Review studies on external variables, such as learner's identity and motivation as affective factors and the impact of culture, on L2 learning. |
| Second language instruction | Introduction to the characteristics of different L2 learning conditions and their corresponding instructions, including classroom learning, immersionlearning, and distance learning |

courses.subject: LING
courses.title: Bilingual Acquisition
courses.description: This course introduces students to the basic concepts and issues in the field of bilingual acquisition. How do children acquire two languages in the first years of life? What are the factors that shape their bilingual development? What is the impact of bilingualism on the bilingual child’s developing cognition and brain? The acquisition of different constructions and domains of grammar in bilingual children will be explored. Similarities and differences between monolingual and bilingual acquisition will also be discussed. Students will have the opportunity to work with language data from bilingual children acquiring Cantonese and English as well as other language pairs.

courses.subject: LING
courses.title: Linguistics and Information Technology
courses.description: This course aims to introduce the applications of linguistics in the field of information technology. The focus of the course is on basic concepts in natural language processing, and ambiguities in human-machine interaction. Through hands-on experience, students will gain a better understanding of the problems with current speech recognition software and natural language processing systems, and of how linguistic knowledge can help provide solutions to some of these problems.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken TRAN2610
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students will be exposed to major topics in the field. The emphasis will be on how linguistic knowledge can augment computational methods in natural language processing tasks. They will be given non-technical introduction to the basic idea/rationale behind the computational algorithms. Students will be able to appreciate the synergy of the field of Linguistics and Computer Science.

2. Students will have a good understanding of the data-oriented methodology, e.g. the use of corpus data, training, testing, and evaluation.

3. Apart from learning the concepts, students will learn to use some user-friendly tools to do some simple text processing and analysis themselves.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Introduction--It provides a general introduction to the significance of IT on linguistics and vice versa. An overview of natural language processing research and practical everyday IT applications will be provided. The strengths and limitations of computers and its implications to language processing will be discussed.

2. Tokenization, stemming and word segmentation--Text processing begins with tokenization of text chunks. While it looks like an easy task, it is a non-trivial task for computers. Special attention will be given to the Chinese word segmentation problem where word boundaries are not explicitly indicated in the Chinese writing system.

3. Part-of-speech (POS) tagging--POS tagging is a task that enhances the information of the text and critically affects further text processing. POS tagging schemes will be reviewed. The bigram approach to tagging will be demonstrated.

4. Corpora-based training and testing--In the last 20 years, the field of natural language processing is dominated by the corpus-oriented approach in all sorts of tasks. This is also an area where linguists’ contribution is important. We will demonstrate how corpora can be used to train and test word segmenter and POS tagger.

5. Tag Cloud / Search Engine -- The bag-of-words model will be introduced as the general representation of text documents. The generic representation enables computers to quantify the relative “importance” of words in texts so that keywords or chunks can be selected for retrieval.

6. Email Spam Filtering / Sentiment Analysis--Despite their superficially very different functions, both applications can be considered to be particular examples of document classification. We will discuss how corpus-based machine learning methods make use of keyword in documents to classify documents into different categories.

7. Speech recognition--Students will be introduced to the basic principle behind the mapping of speech signals to words. Concepts include formant, spectrum, Fourier transformation, etc. Statistical strategy (just the idea, not the math) to recover words from phones will be examined.

courses.subject: LING
courses.title: Topics in Bilingualism & Bilingual Acquisition
courses.description: This course explores current topics in bilingualism and bilingual acquisition from both theoretical and methodological perspectives. Issues at the interface of bilingualism and language acquisition in bilingual and multilingual contexts will be addressed. The emphasis of the course will be on individual bilingualism: how do children acquire, process and represent two or more languages in early childhood? What is the relationship between language and cognitive development in bilingual children? Central questions in bilingual acquisition and methodological issues in investigating bilingual infants and children will be discussed. The development of bilingual and trilingual children in Hong Kong and overseas communities will be the focus of our discussion. Issues regarding how heritage speakers in North America and UK develop their heritage language and undergo language shift will also be discussed.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MPhil-PhD Linguistics, MPhil Linguistics or PhD Linguistics
courses.learning_outcomes:
 develop a good grasp of the theoretical and empirical issues in bilingualism and bilingual acquisition
 identify and address research questions, taking an interdisciplinary perspective on the field of bilingualism and bilingual acquisition
 appreciate the important relationship between linguistic theory and acquisition research and the centrality of language acquisition in relation to other areas of linguistics
 develop the ability to conduct a small-scale research project on a topic in bilingual acquisition by using the databases in CHILDES or piloting an experimental study
 raise students’ awareness of the complexity of bilingualism and bilingual acquisition and deepen their appreciation of children’s ability to acquire two or more languages
 develop ability to learn, discuss with peers and benefit from peer support
courses.course_syllabus:
 Theoretical issues in bilingualism and bilingual acquisition
How do bilinguals acquire, process and represent the target languages? How do bilinguals differ from monolinguals?

 Methods and methodological issues in bilingual acquisition
methods of data collection, developmental stages, corpus construction; elicitation; comparisons of monolingual and bilingual development

 language dominance
how to measure language dominance, significance of language dominance

 Crosslinguistic influence
theories of crosslinguistic influence, direction of transfer, bidirectional influence,

 Role of input and experience in bilingual and multilingual acquisition
quality and quantity of input, properties of input across diverse bilingual and multilingual contexts, linear vs non-linear views of input

 Heritage bilingualism
heritage language acquisition in children and adults, language shift and maintenance, incomplete acquisition, language attrition

 Languages in contact
diversity of world’s languages, endangered languages, contact varieties of English, e.g. Singapore Colloquial English and Chinese Pidgin English

 Bilingualism and cognition
the bilingual advantage in children and adults, cognitive advantages of bilingual children and adults

courses.subject: LING
courses.title: Topics in Sign Linguistics
courses.description: Linguistic inquiry into sign language structure reveals universal principles of linguistic organization shared by sign languages and spoken languages, in phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics and pragmatics. Additionally, similar processes of language acquisition are observed when children acquire sign language in monolingual and bilingual contexts. Yet, differences in modality of communication, auditory versus visual, pose challenges to researchers in their attempts to account for the role of space and gesture in the organization of sign language grammar and language acquisition. This introductory course aims to address these issues.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MPhil-PhD Linguistics, MPhil Linguistics or PhD Linguistics
courses.learning_outcomes:
After completing the course, students will achieve some fundamental understanding of:

1. Signed and spoken languages share principles and constraints of linguistic organization at different levels
2. There are modality effects and non-effects in sign language structure and acquisition
courses.course_syllabus:
Modality of communication
It refers to the medium through which linguistic signals are transmitted to achieve a communicative outcome. The medium, oral versus signed, may lead to interesting linguistic and processing consequences

Spatial grammar
A term often adopted by sign linguists to refer to how sign languages use space in the construction of grammar

Verb Typology
Sign languages display an interesting phenomenon of classifying verbs according to whether they use space or not and whether the verbal root is comprised, instead of a conglomeration of phonological components, movement or handshape, depending on the theoretical approach one adopts. In the literature, verbs in signed languages can be roughly classified into plain verbs, spatial verbs, agreement verbs and classifier verbs.

Code-blending
It is a form of code-mixing phenomena where signers ‘stack’ elements of both sign language and spoken language simultaneously in language production. It also implies that signers may access two grammars not only in production, but also comprehension, as shown by empirical findings in bilingual processing research.

courses.subject: LING
courses.title: Technologies in Linguistic Research I
courses.description: This course is a continuation of LING 6980 (Research Methodology). Students will learn selected techonologies in contemporary linguistic research. Topics may include EEG, fMRI, eye-tracking, advanced behavioral methods and data analytics and computational mathematics. Students will learn hands-on techniques and will complete a research project using the methods introduced.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Pre-requisite: LING6980;For students in MPhil-PhD Linguistics, MPhil Linguistics or PhD Linguistics
courses.learning_outcomes: Upon successfully completing the subject, students should be able to describe the techniques introduced, understand the parameters involved, conduct research using the techniques, and critically evaluate their purpose, advantages and limitations.
courses.course_syllabus: The content of the course varies depending on the research techniques to be covered by the instructor
courses.feedback_evaluation: Students are welcome to give comments and feedback by sending them in written form to the instructor.
courses.required_readings:
Goodwin, C.J. (2013). Research in Psychology: Methods and Designs. *Wiley: NJ.*

Gibson, E. and Fedorenko, E. (2010) Weak quantitative standards in linguistics research. Trends Cogn. Sci. 14, 233–234

Drost, E. A. (2011). Validity and reliability in social science research. *Education Research and Perspective*, 38, 105–123.

Abbuhl, R., Gass, S., & Mackey, A. (2013). Experimental research design. Chapter 7, In R. J. Podesva & D. Sharma (eds). Research Methods in Linguistics. *Cambridge University Press: NY*.

Kaiser, E. (2013). Experimental paradigms in psycholinguistics. In R. J. Podesva & D. Sharma (eds). Research Methods in Linguistics. *Cambridge University Press: NY*.

P.C. Gomez (2013). Statistical Methods in Language and Linguistic Research*. Equinox: CT*. [Chapters 1-3]

Kemmerer D. 2014. Cognitive Neuroscience of Language: Psychology Press. (PART I)

Luck, S. J. (2014). An introduction to the event-related potential technique. MIT Press.

Almajidy, R. K., Mankodiya, K., Abtahi, M., & Hofmann, U. G. (2019). A newcomer's guide to functional near infrared spectroscopy experiments. IEEE Reviews in Biomedical Engineering, 13, 292-308.

Spapé, M., Verdonschot, R., & Van Steenbergen, H. (2020). The E-Primer: An introduction to creating psychological experiments in E-Prime. Leiden University Press.

Gazzaniga et al. (2002). The Methods of Cognitive Neuroscience (Chapter 4). Cognitive Neuroscience: The Biology of the Mind.
courses.recommended_readings:
Hanselman, D., & Littlefield, B. (2005). Mastering Matlab 7. Pearson Prentice Hall: NJ. [Chapters 1-2]
Kaiser, E. (2013). Experimental paradigms in psycholinguistics. In R. J. Podesva & D. Sharma (eds). Research Methods in Linguistics. Cambridge University Press: NY.

Gibson & Fedorenko (2013). The need for quantitative methods in syntax and semantics research. Language & Cognitive Processes. 1-2, 88-124.

Sprouse, Schuetze, & Almeida (2013). A comparison of informal and formal acceptability judgments using a random sample from Linguistic Inquiry 2001-2010. Lingua. 134, 219-248.

courses.title: Topics in Statistics
courses.description: Students will learn selected statistical techniques in contemporary research in linguistics. Topics may include multiple regression, discriminant analysis, and linear mixed-effects model.

Johnson, K. (2008). Quantitative Methods in Linguistics. Blackwell Publishing: MA.
